sources.claim: C++ tests assert observable contracts across normal, boundary, failure, lifetime, and exception cases without coupling unnecessarily to private representation.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Good tests check **observable behaviour through the public interface**: what a function returns, what an object reports, what exceptions it throws. They don't check private helper call order. Cover four kinds of case: **normal**, **boundary** (0, 1, maximum, empty, exactly full), **failure** (invalid input, errors, exceptions), and **lifetime** (copies stay independent, moved-from objects stay valid). Name each test after the behaviour it proves. **Coverage** tells you which lines ran, not whether the results were checked or the edge cases exist. **Unit tests** check one piece; **integration tests** check pieces working together, like parsing a real file end to end.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner's parser tests reach 95% line coverage, all green. A user enters "0" and the app accepts an order of zero items, because no test checked the boundary: the tests only ran the code without asserting results. A parser test covers empty, valid, boundary, and malformed input and checks returned value or error rather than private helper call order. In this lesson you'll create a focused automated test suite with normal, boundary and failure cases.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Conceptual constraints and diagnostics**, **Exceptions and guarantees**, **Streams, files and parsing** and **Class interface and invariants**.

sections.heading: The rule: assert behaviour across case kinds
One test, one behaviour

includes: Write tests for normal, boundary, failure and lifetime behaviour through public interfaces.
Explain why coverage alone doesn't prove a contract, and distinguish unit from integration tests.
excludes: Property-based and fuzz testing in depth.

outcomes: Create a focused automated test suite with normal, boundary and failure cases.

examples.title: Testing parse_quantity
examples.situation: A parser test covers empty, valid, boundary, and malformed input and checks returned value or error rather than private helper call order.
walkthrough: **Covers empty, valid, boundary, and malformed input:** "", "3", "1"/"99"/"0"/"100", "two"/"3x".
**Checks returned value or error:** each assert compares the optional result.
**Rather than private helper call order:** the tests only use parse_quantity's public signature, so refactoring its internals will not break them.
examples.result: The zero-quantity bug is caught, and the suite survives refactoring.

examples.title: The integration gap
examples.situation: Every unit test passes, but reading orders.txt with Windows line endings rejects every line.
walkthrough: Add an integration test that runs the reader on a sample file with CRLF endings.
Fix parsing to ignore trailing whitespace, and keep both tests.
examples.result: Real files work, and the fix is locked in by a test.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: High line coverage proves the class contract and every edge case are correct.
misconceptions.correction: Coverage only records which lines ran. Without assertions on results and deliberately chosen boundary and failure cases, bugs pass with full coverage.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, why did 95% coverage miss the zero-quantity bug?

analogy.example: Coverage is like **a guard's patrol log showing every room was visited**. It doesn't say whether they checked the windows were locked (assertions) or tried the weak ones (boundaries). A good test suite is **a checklist of specific locks to try**.
limitations: Guards patrol rooms; tests should check behaviours.
Integration tests check the whole building's alarm.

remediation.explanation: For each function list **one normal, the boundaries, and each failure mode**, then write one named test per behaviour that asserts the observable result.

recap.summary: To create a focused test suite, test observable behaviour through public interfaces, cover normal, boundary, failure and lifetime cases with explicit assertions, name one test per behaviour, add integration tests for real inputs, and treat coverage as a hint rather than proof.
